hints: Recall what adds to ethanal in reaction 1 with HCN and NaCN, and which two groups become attached to the carbonyl carbon.
walkthrough:
Spot the cyanohydrin reaction**
You start with ethanal, $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CHO}$. With HCN and NaCN you are adding HCN across the $\text{C=O}$ bond. The $\text{CN}$ group adds to the carbonyl carbon and the $\text{H}$ adds to the oxygen to give an OH group, so the product P is $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH(OH)CN}$.

Draw displayed correctly**
Displayed means show every atom and every bond. Draw $\text{H}-\text{C}(\text{H})(\text{H})-\text{C}(\text{OH})(\text{H})-\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$. Check the middle carbon has four single bonds to $\text{CH}_{3}$, $\text{OH}$, $\text{H}$ and $\text{CN}$.

Final answer: Displayed formula: $\text{H}-\overset{\text{H}}{\overset{|}{\text{C}}}-\overset{\text{OH}}{\overset{|}{\text{C}}}(\text{H})-\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$ i.e. $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH(OH)CN}$ shown with all bonds and all H, OH and CN groups displayed.

hints: Compare Q, $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH(OH)CO}_{2}\text{H}$, with R, $\text{CH}_{2}=\text{CHCO}_{2}\text{H}$, and identify the small molecule lost.
walkthrough:
Compare structures Q and R**
Look closely: Q has $\text{CH}_{3}-\text{CH(OH)}-$ while R has $\text{CH}_{2}=\text{CH}-$. You have lost H from one carbon and OH from the next to form a $\text{C=C}$ double bond. That loss of $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$ from a single molecule is dehydration, a type of elimination.
Final answer: Dehydration (elimination of water).

hints: Identify the functional group change from Q to S at the middle carbon, from $\text{CH(OH)}$ to $\text{C=O}$, and think what happens to hydrogen.
walkthrough:
Recognise secondary alcohol to ketone**
In Q the group is $\text{CH}_{3}-\text{CH(OH)}-\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$, a secondary alcohol. In S it is $\text{CH}_{3}-\text{CO}-\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$, a ketone plus carboxylic acid. Only the alcohol is oxidised, the $\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$ is unchanged.

Balance with [O] and water**
Oxidation is shown as $+ [\text{O}]$. You remove two H atoms from $\text{CH(OH)}$ to make $\text{C=O}$, and those combine with $[\text{O}]$ to give $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$. So write $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH(OH)CO}_{2}\text{H} + [\text{O}] \rightarrow \text{CH}_{3}\text{COCO}_{2}\text{H} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O}$.

hints: Recall the standard orange oxidising agent used in AS chemistry to oxidise a secondary alcohol to a ketone under acidic conditions.
walkthrough:
Choose the correct oxidant**
For oxidation of a secondary alcohol shown by $[\text{O}]$, the laboratory reagent is dichromate(VI) in acid. State $\text{K}_{2}\text{Cr}_{2}\text{O}_{7}$ or $\text{Na}_{2}\text{Cr}_{2}\text{O}_{7}$ plus dilute $\text{H}_{2}\text{SO}_{4}$. Heating under reflux completes the oxidation to the ketone S.

Final answer: Acidified potassium dichromate(VI) or sodium dichromate(VI): $\text{K}_{2}\text{Cr}_{2}\text{O}_{7}$ or $\text{Na}_{2}\text{Cr}_{2}\text{O}_{7}$ with dilute $\text{H}_{2}\text{SO}_{4}$ (or $\text{H}^{+}(\text{aq})$), heated.

hints: Think of your left and right hands as mirror images and ask whether one can be placed exactly on top of the other.
walkthrough:
Picture mirror images**
Optical isomers come in pairs. Hold one isomer up to a mirror and you see the other. Crucially you cannot rotate one to fit exactly on top of the other, just like left and right hands. That property is called non-superimposable mirror images.
Final answer: Molecules that are non-superimposable mirror images of each other.

hints: Locate the chiral carbon in Q, $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH(OH)CO}_{2}\text{H}$, and list its four different groups.
Recall how to show 3D shape with a solid wedge for a bond coming out and a hashed wedge for a bond going back, keeping the other two bonds in the plane.
walkthrough:
Find the chiral centre**
Look at Q: $\text{H}_{3}\text{C}-\text{C}(\text{OH})(\text{H})-\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$. The middle carbon is bonded to four different groups: $\text{CH}_{3}$, $\text{OH}$, $\text{H}$ and $\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$. That is your stereocentre.

Draw a correct pair of mirror images**
Draw the central C with two bonds in the plane, e.g. $\text{CH}_{3}$ and $\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$. Then for isomer 1 put $\text{OH}$ on a solid wedge (out) and $\text{H}$ on a hashed wedge (back). For isomer 2 swap them: $\text{OH}$ on dash and $\text{H}$ on wedge. Check they are mirror images and cannot be superimposed.

Final answer: Two 3D structures of $\text{CH}_{3}-\text{C}^{*}(\text{H})(\text{OH})-\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$ that are mirror images: central C with $\text{CH}_{3}$, $\text{OH}$, $\text{H}$ and $\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$, one isomer with OH on wedge and H on dash, the other with OH on dash and H on wedge.

hints: Start from R, $\text{CH}_{2}=\text{CHCO}_{2}\text{H}$, and recall how the $\text{C=C}$ opens to give the repeat unit of an addition polymer.
Think what happens to a carboxylic acid group when it reacts with aqueous NaOH.
Remember to show continuation bonds through the backbone carbons and to place the sodium salt group correctly on the repeat unit.
walkthrough:
Form the intermediate addition polymer**
R is propenoic acid, $\text{CH}_{2}=\text{CHCO}_{2}\text{H}$. In addition polymerisation the $\text{C=C}$ opens and links: $\text{-CH}_{2}-\text{CH(CO}_{2}\text{H})-$ repeated. Draw the backbone with two carbons, each with two chain bonds continuing left and right.

Convert acid to sodium salt**
NaOH(aq) neutralises the $\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$ group: $\text{CO}_{2}\text{H} + \text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{CO}_{2}\text{Na} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O}$. So replace $\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$ by $\text{CO}_{2}\text{Na}$. The backbone stays $\text{-CH}_{2}-\text{CH}-$.

Present one repeat unit clearly**
Draw $\text{-CH}_{2}-\text{CH(CO}_{2}\text{Na})-$ with brackets and continuation bonds outside. Show two H on the $\text{CH}_{2}$, one H on the $\text{CH}$, and $\text{CO}_{2}\text{Na}$ attached to that CH. This is W.

Final answer: Repeat unit of W: $\text{-CH}_{2}\text{-CH(CO}_{2}\text{Na)-}$ shown with continuation bonds at each end through the chain carbons, i.e. backbone $\text{-CH}_{2}-\text{CH}-$ with $\text{CO}_{2}\text{Na}$ attached to the CH and H atoms completing tetravalency.

hints: Classify intermediate I and intermediate II as secondary or primary carbocations by counting alkyl groups on the $\text{C}^{+}$.
Recall how alkyl groups push electron density toward a positive centre and what this does to the spread of charge.
walkthrough:
Compare the carbocations**
Intermediate I is $(\text{CH}_{3})_{2}\text{C}^{+}\text{H}$, the $\text{C}^{+}$ is joined to two $\text{CH}_{3}$ groups, a secondary carbocation. Intermediate II is $^{+}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$, the $\text{C}^{+}$ is joined to only one alkyl group, a primary carbocation.

Link alkyl groups to stability**
Alkyl groups are electron donating by the positive inductive effect. They push electron density toward the electron deficient $\text{C}^{+}$. With two alkyl groups, I spreads and reduces the positive charge more effectively than II with one group. Greater stabilisation means I forms preferentially.

Final answer: Intermediate I has more alkyl (electron donating) groups attached to the $\text{C}^{+}$ than II, giving a greater positive inductive effect. This stabilises the positive charge by spreading / delocalising it, so I is more stable and more likely to form.

hints: Recall that the $\text{C=C}$ pi bond acts as the nucleophile attacking the $\delta^{+}$ end of HBr in the first step.
Think how the $\text{H-Br}$ bond breaks and where the shared pair goes, and why you must show $\text{H}^{\delta^{+}}-\text{Br}^{\delta^{-}}$.
Consider what nucleophile attacks the carbocation in the second step and where its lone pair arrow starts and ends.
walkthrough:
Attack on polarised HBr**
Show $\text{H}^{\delta^{+}}-\text{Br}^{\delta^{-}}$ because Br is more electronegative. Draw a curly arrow starting at the $\text{C=C}$ double bond of Z, $\text{H}_{2}\text{C}=\text{CHCH}_{3}$, pointing to the $\text{H}$ of HBr. At the same time draw a second curly arrow from the $\text{H-Br}$ bond to Br. This forms the secondary carbocation I and $\text{Br}^{-}$.

Capture of the carbocation**
Now the $\text{Br}^{-}$ has lone pairs. Draw a curly arrow from a lone pair on $\text{Br}^{-}$ directly to the $\text{C}^{+}$ centre of intermediate I. This makes the $\text{C-Br}$ bond and gives product T, $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CHBrCH}_{3}$.

Check mechanism details**
Ensure arrows start at electron rich centres (double bond, bond pair, lone pair) and end at electron poor centres ($\text{H}^{\delta^{+}}$, Br, $\text{C}^{+}$). Include all charges, dipoles and lone pairs on $\text{Br}^{-}$.

Final answer: Step 1: curly arrow from $\text{C=C}$ to $\text{H}$ of $\text{H}^{\delta^{+}}-\text{Br}^{\delta^{-}}$; curly arrow from $\text{H-Br}$ bond to Br to form $\text{Br}^{-}$ and secondary carbocation. Step 2: curly arrow from lone pair on $\text{Br}^{-}$ to $\text{C}^{+}$ to give $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CHBrCH}_{3}$.

hints: Note that Br in T is replaced by $\text{NH}_{2}$ using $\text{NH}_{3}$ in ethanol.
walkthrough:
Identify substitution by ammonia**
In T, $\text{C-Br}$ becomes $\text{C-NH}_{2}$. The nucleophile $\text{NH}_{3}$ replaces the leaving group $\text{Br}$. That exchange of one group for another at a saturated carbon is nucleophilic substitution.
Final answer: Nucleophilic substitution.

hints: Recall that $\text{LiAlH}_{4}$ reduces both ketones to secondary alcohols and carboxylic acids to primary alcohols.
Count the total [H] atoms needed to convert $\text{CH}_{3}\text{COCO}_{2}\text{H}$ to $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH(OH)CH}_{2}\text{OH}$ plus water and balance the equation.
walkthrough:
Predict the organic product**
S is $\text{CH}_{3}-\text{CO}-\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$. $\text{LiAlH}_{4}$ is a strong reducer. The ketone $\text{C=O}$ gains $2[\text{H}]$ to become $\text{CH(OH)}$, and the acid $\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$ gains $4[\text{H}]$ to become $\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH}$. So the product is $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH(OH)CH}_{2}\text{OH}$.

Balance with [H] and water**
Adding up H: you need $6[\text{H}]$ on the left. Oxygen balance gives one $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$ on the right. Write $\text{CH}_{3}\text{COCO}_{2}\text{H} + 6[\text{H}] \rightarrow \text{CH}_{3}\text{CH(OH)CH}_{2}\text{OH} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O}$.

hints: Start from Na atomic number 11 and remove one electron to form $\text{Na}^{+}$.
walkthrough:
Remove the outer electron**
Na is $1\text{s}^{2}2\text{s}^{2}2\text{p}^{6}3\text{s}^{1}$. Forming $\text{Na}^{+}$ loses the $3\text{s}^{1}$ electron, leaving the stable neon configuration $1\text{s}^{2}2\text{s}^{2}2\text{p}^{6}$.

hints: Think what happens to the number of occupied shells as you go from $\text{Li}^{+}$ to $\text{Na}^{+}$ to $\text{K}^{+}$.
walkthrough:
Add shells down the group**
Going down Group 1 each new element adds a new principal shell. Even though nuclear charge increases, the outer electrons are further from the nucleus with more inner shielding, so the ionic radius increases.
Final answer: Ions have more (occupied) electron shells / energy levels down the group.
